title: private-deploy - vpc peering / dns / tls / egress debug notes
content:
Goal: Track the breadcrumbs for the networking incident affecting private deployments in us-west-2 (customer staging). Symptoms: API calls from customer pod to hosted control-plane intermittently fail with TLS handshake errors and DNS resolution timeouts. Some pods succeed, others fail - looks like not persistent per-instance.

Summary of what I observed:
- Failures started after we rotated a peering route table and applied a more restrictive egress ACL on the private subnets (trying to lock down outbound to only necessary control-plane IPs).
- Errors: kubectl logs from service pod show repeated DNS lookup timeouts and openssl s_client hiccups.

Commands tried and outputs (captured):
1) Check VPC peering status (aws cli)
$ aws ec2 describe-vpc-peering-connections --filters Name=status-code,Values=active
-> shows peering connection pcx-0abcde12345 active, accepter-vpc-id vpc-0aaaa, requester-vpc-id vpc-0bbbb

2) Route tables (from the node subnet route table)
$ aws ec2 describe-route-tables --filters Name=vpc-id,Values=vpc-0aaaa --query 'RouteTables[*].Routes'
-> route to 10.0.0.0/16 (peer VPC) via pcx-0abcde OK
-> default route 0.0.0.0/0 -> igw-0ccc (should be fine for egress to internet)

3) Traceroute from an affected pod to control-plane endpoint (10.51.12.34)
$ kubectl exec -it pod-xyz -- traceroute -n 10.51.12.34
1  10.0.1.1  0.5 ms
2  10.254.3.2  1.1 ms
3  10.51.12.34  2.0 ms
(no obvious routing hop failure)

4) DNS resolution from pod (failing case):
$ kubectl exec pod-bad -- nslookup controlplane.redwood-inference.internal
;; connection timed out; no servers could be reached

But from another pod (good):
$ kubectl exec pod-good -- nslookup controlplane.redwood-inference.internal
Server: 10.0.0.2
Address: 10.0.0.2#53
Name: controlplane.redwood-inference.internal
Address: 10.51.12.34

So DNS server (kube-dns / coredns) sometimes unreachable from some pods. Hypothesis: egress ACLs or host-level iptables interfering with pod -> node -> coredns path, or ENI level source/dest checks.

5) Inspect iptables on node (quick capture):
$ ssh ec2-user@node-12 (node hosting pod-bad)
$ sudo iptables -S | grep 53 || true
-A OUTPUT -p udp --dport 53 -j ACCEPT
-A OUTPUT -p tcp --dport 53 -j ACCEPT
(appears ok)

6) Check security group outbound rules for node ENI and customer subnet:
- Node SG has outbound 0.0.0.0/0 (All traffic) -> OK
- Customer-managed egress ACL was recently changed: inbound/outbound rules are stateless; I see a DENY on outbound to 10.0.0.0/8 in one ACL entry (rule #150) that is higher priority than the allow for specific control-plane IPs. That could block traffic to core DNS if DNS is in 10.0.0.0/8.

7) TLS handshake test to control plane from failing pod:
$ kubectl exec pod-bad -- openssl s_client -connect controlplane.redwood-inference.internal:443 -servername controlplane.redwood-inference.internal -brief
CONNECTED(00000003)
139705XXX:error:14077410:SSL routines:SSL23_GET_SERVER_HELLO:sslv3 alert certificate unknown:c
...
(weird: cert mismatch? but from pod-good TLS works)

8) Capture iptables nat on node-good vs node-bad: noticed node-bad has extra custom chain introduced by CNI plugin plugin-x for egress policies; might be mis-applying to host networking.

Hypotheses (ordered):
1) Egress Network ACL misconfiguration: there is a deny rule that blocks traffic to some internal CIDR ranges (10.0.0.0/8) and that is affecting DNS (which lives in that range for some clusters). This would intermittently affect pods depending on node's subnet association.
2) CNI plugin bug: egress-policy chain is applied inconsistently across nodes; older nodes with plugin-x v1.2.1 behave differently than new nodes with v1.3.0. The chain is dropping some packets to port 53 and also manipulating TLS SNI passthrough.
3) Source/dest check or ENI route mismatch after peering change: some routes still send traffic to NAT which strips SNI or rewrites source, causing cert checks to fail. Less likely but possible.
4) DNS caching + TTL + kube-dns replicas: if kube-dns endpoints live on a subset of nodes and egress ACL blocks traffic from certain subnets, pods scheduled on those nodes will fail resolution.

Quick reproduction steps I ran:
- Recreate pod on affected node (kubectl delete pod && kubectl get pod -o wide to ensure node) -> reproduced.
- Move pod to a node in a subnet with different ACL -> OK.
- Temporarily add allow ALL outbound on subnet ACL -> problem disappears (strong indicator ACL issue).

Immediate mitigation applied:
- Rolled back the ACL change (removed the deny 10.0.0.0/8 rule) for staging customer VPC subnets at 2026-02-24 14:23 PST. Verified DNS/TLS success across pods.
- Filed change request to revisit egress rules with more specific allows (do not use broad denies).

Open action items / next steps:
- [ ] Create a smoke test that validates pod -> coredns (UDP/TCP 53), and pod -> control-plane (443) across all nodes after any ACL/route change. Put in infra PR. (owner: Samir)
- [ ] Add egress ACL preflight checklist to Confluence (link in linked_artifacts). (owner: Lina)
- [ ] Investigate CNI versions across nodes and run controlled upgrade on a small canary pool to see if egress chains differ. (owner: Maya)
- [ ] Review VPC peering route propagation and confirm no overlapping CIDR that would trigger ACL deny matches. (owner: Network Eng)

Notes / things I tried but later rolled back:
- Forced dnsPolicy: Default on pod to ignore kube-dns -> didn't help, still failed on nodes where ACL blocked 53 outbound.
- Changing kube-proxy mode -> too disruptive, rolled back.

Useful logs / snippets saved in case we need them:
- CloudTrail change record for network ACL update: https://console.aws.amazon.com/cloudtrail/home?region=us-west-2#events
- Node iptables dump (node-bad) saved to /tmp/node-bad-iptables-20260224.log (on my laptop).

Bottom line: Root cause highly likely misconfigured network ACL (egress deny) combined with node scheduling that put pods on subnets with that deny. TLS errors are a secondary effect (probably due to failed SNI handshake or partial connection resets when traffic is dropped mid-handshake). Recommending stricter review before ACL changes and automated post-change checks.

Timestamps:
- 2026-02-24 13:18 PST: ACL change applied (by infra-runbook)
- 2026-02-24 13:45 PST: First alerts from staging customer (dns timeouts)
- 2026-02-24 14:23 PST: Rolled back ACL change -> incidents cleared by 14:30

If anyone wants to poke at the environment: staging cluster name: redwood-staging-usw2-private-1, control-plane IP: 10.51.12.34.

Random notes: put a short bash script in infra repo to check ACL rules and ensure no broad "10.0.0.0/8 deny" rules exist. Will open PR referencing ENG-4821.

-- Samir
